A few things before you start planning. First, do not try to memorise the whole thing. Students who memorise stop breathing after two minutes and then they panic. Learn your outline instead, and let the sentences happen. Second, I want you to practise standing up, out loud, at home. Reading it silently is not rehearsing, it is reading. Third, and this is the one everybody ignores: decide how you are going to finish before you decide how you are going to start. People remember the last twenty seconds. And if you run out of time, do not speed up. Skip a slide and keep your ending. Nobody has ever complained about a presentation that finished early.

Hey, it's Sam. So mine was today and it did not go how I expected, so I'm telling you before yours. I spent about four hours making the slides look nice and about fifteen minutes practising the actual talking, and you can guess which of those two things mattered. I forgot to look up. I read the screen for eleven minutes and I have no idea if anybody was listening. Also I planned to finish with the good part, and then I ran out of time and I skipped it, which is the one thing you should never skip. If I did it again I'd practise standing up in my room, out loud, with the door closed, and I'd stop caring about the font.

Lais writes the outline before she opens the slides. She decides how the presentation is going to finish and works backwards from there. She rehearses standing up, out loud, three times in her room. On the day she looks up at the audience instead of reading the screen. She finishes twenty seconds early and takes two questions.
